findings.source_passage: the whale looked like a portly burgher smoking his pipe of a warm afternoon. But that pipe, poor whale, was thy last.
findings.source_locator: paragraph describing the whale's first appearance at the surface
findings.why_it_matters: The 'warm afternoon' detail and the full simile create the ironic domestic-vs.-doom juxtaposition that is signature Melville; losing 'of a warm afternoon' flattens the tonal contrast.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'of a warm afternoon' to the burgher-pipe simile to preserve the ironic register.

findings.source_passage: "Woo-hoo! Wa-hee!" screamed the Gay-Header in reply, raising some old war-whoop to the skies; as every oarsman in the strained boat involuntarily bounced forward with the one tremendous leading stroke which the eager Indian gave.
findings.why_it_matters: The source attributes the cry to 'the Gay-Header' (Tashtego) and includes the kinetic description of every oarsman bouncing forward — a moment of collective physical animation. The draft simply lists the three cries in sequence without the explanatory surrounding prose, losing the cause-and-effect energy.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the attribution 'the Gay-Header' and the image of oarsmen bouncing forward from the leading stroke after Tashtego's war-whoop.

findings.source_passage: "Ka-la! Koo-loo!" howled Queequeg, as if smacking his lips over a mouthful of Grenadier's steak.
findings.why_it_matters: The cannibal simile ('smacking his lips over a mouthful of Grenadier's steak') is a defining character note for Queequeg and a flash of Melville's dark comedy; its omission erases the interpretive texture of the moment.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'as if smacking his lips over a mouthful of Grenadier's steak' after Queequeg's howl.

findings.source_passage: the tall form of Tashtego at the steering oar crouching almost double, in order to bring down his centre of gravity
findings.source_locator: description of the boat under the taut harpoon-line
findings.why_it_matters: The draft incorrectly reassigns this image to 'the tall Gay-Header' (which is accurate) but omits 'at the steering oar' and 'almost double,' reducing the specificity and physical vividness of the scene.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'at the steering oar crouching almost double' to retain precision.

findings.source_passage: and vehement puff after puff from the mouth of the excited headsman; as at every dart, hauling in upon his crooked lance (by the line attached to it), Stubb straightened it again and again
findings.source_locator: description of Stubb during the blood-tide passage
findings.why_it_matters: The parenthetical '(by the line attached to it)' is a characteristic Melville technical aside that grounds the action in seamanship; its omission slightly reduces the documentary texture.
findings.suggested_fix: Minor; restore the parenthetical on revision if word budget allows.

summary: The draft is largely faithful and preserves most major signature passages verbatim, but three medium-severity voice-flattenings (the 'warm afternoon' burgher simile, the Gay-Header's war-whoop sequence, and the Grenadier's-steak simile for Queequeg) cumulatively thin the chapter's ironic and comic register.
